drafted.title: Missing input validation on agent tool-call and model-serving parameters
drafted.description: Agent-adjacent components — MCP/tool servers, workflow/pipeline nodes, and model-serving or inference backends — accept externally- or model-controlled parameters (file paths, flow/node configs, gRPC/HTTP request fields, tensor shapes, header values) without validating their type, bounds, or structure before acting on them. Because agent frameworks route untrusted, often model-generated or multi-hop input directly into these dependencies, a single unchecked field anywhere in the toolchain lets an attacker crash the service (DoS), bypass a security or sandbox check, or pivot a malformed value into injection-driven remote code execution.

drafted.title: File disclosure and SSRF via unrestricted XML external entity references in document/tool parsers
drafted.description: An agent tool, connector, or ingestion library parses attacker-influenced XML-bearing content (uploaded documents, SAML/SOAP messages, SVG/DOCX/PDF payloads, config or API responses) with DTD processing and external entity resolution left enabled, so a crafted <!ENTITY> or external DTD reference is resolved by the parser. This lets an attacker who controls any document or message the agent ingests exfiltrate local files, pivot an SSRF request into internal services/cloud metadata endpoints, or exhaust resources via entity-expansion (billion laughs) denial of service, all without needing code execution or valid credentials.

drafted.title: Downstream injection via unneutralized LLM or tool-relayed input
drafted.description: Agent frameworks and MCP tool servers often forward externally-sourced or LLM-generated strings (file paths, tool arguments, crawled web text, query fragments) straight into a downstream interpreter — a shell, SQL/Cypher engine, template renderer, log sink, or the agent's own chat-markup parser — without neutralizing special characters or control tokens. Because the agent treats this data as trusted once it crosses the tool/LLM boundary, an attacker who controls any upstream input (a tool argument, a web page the agent reads, a filename) can smuggle commands, queries, or role-boundary-forging tokens that execute arbitrary code, escalate privileges, or hijack the agent's context.

drafted.title: Open redirect to attacker-controlled host via unvalidated redirect parameter
drafted.description: An agent-adjacent web front-end, OAuth/login flow, or tool (e.g. MCP OAuth dynamic client registration, logout/login handlers, webhook or transfer tools) accepts a client-supplied URL parameter or Host header and redirects, issues tokens, or sends sensitive output to it without validating the destination against an allow-list. Attackers exploit the trusted domain to craft phishing links that steal OAuth authorization codes, session tokens, or exfiltrate agent-generated data to attacker-controlled infrastructure, undermining the identity-delegation trust the redirect step was meant to uphold.

drafted.title: Unauthenticated cross-origin tool invocation via missing origin/host validation
drafted.description: An MCP/agent server trusts the source of an incoming request without verifying the Origin, Host, or token-audience binding of the connection, so a malicious web page, DNS-rebinding attacker, or unrelated third-party service can drive a browser or network client into issuing requests that the local or remote agent tool server accepts as legitimate. This lets an attacker silently invoke privileged agent tools, read or mutate connected systems (files, databases, smart devices, SaaS accounts), or complete OAuth/token flows on the victim's behalf, entirely without presenting valid credentials.

drafted.title: Directory traversal via unsanitized file-path parameters in agent tool endpoints
drafted.description: An attacker embeds '../' or backslash dot-dot sequences inside a filename, model name, extension name, or path parameter accepted by an agent-adjacent tool/API endpoint (e.g. model download, extension install, settings apply, log viewer, archive extraction), causing the backend to resolve the path outside its intended base directory. This lets the attacker read or overwrite arbitrary files on the host, and when the written file is itself loaded as code (a plugin, extension, or extracted archive entry), the traversal escalates to remote code execution.

drafted.title: Arbitrary code execution via unsandboxed eval of agent-generated expressions
drafted.description: An agent framework feeds untrusted input — LLM tool-call arguments, generated code, workflow expressions, or templated fields — directly into a dynamic code evaluator such as eval()/exec() or an insufficiently sandboxed expression engine, letting an attacker who controls that input (via prompt injection, a malicious tool response, or a crafted workflow payload) run arbitrary code with the host process's privileges. This breaks the isolation agent builders assume exists between 'data the model reasons about' and 'code the runtime executes', turning routine tool-call parsing, custom-component execution, or expression-based automation into full remote code execution.

drafted.title: Path traversal via unsanitized file-path parameters in agent tool endpoints
drafted.description: An agent-exposed tool, model-serving endpoint, or MCP-adjacent service accepts a filename or path parameter (e.g. for upload, save/load, delete, or artifact-fetch operations) and uses it to build a filesystem path without canonicalizing or restricting it to an allowed directory, so an attacker-controlled value containing '../' sequences (or an absolute path/symlink) lets the resolved path escape the intended sandbox. Because these endpoints are often invoked autonomously with the tool's own filesystem privileges, this enables arbitrary file read, write, or delete outside the intended directory — leaking secrets, overwriting configs/plugins, or achieving remote code execution.

drafted.title: Unrestricted file type upload leading to remote code execution
drafted.description: Agent-adjacent software (chatbot web UIs, MCP servers, RAG ingestion pipelines) exposes a file-upload tool or endpoint — for attachments, avatars, media, model artifacts, or 'send file to AI' features — without enforcing a strict allowlist on extension, MIME type, and content; an attacker uploads a script or web shell (e.g. .php, .phar, disguised via MIME/extension mismatch) into a web-accessible or interpreter-reachable directory, and the server later executes it, yielding full remote code execution on the host running the agent and any tools/credentials it has access to.

drafted.title: Execution guardrail bypass via incomplete denylist input validation
drafted.description: An agent tool's safety gate (code sandbox validator, SQL checker, command-approval filter, or deserialization blocklist) permits execution unless input matches a hardcoded list of disallowed tokens, functions, modules, or syntax; because such denylists are inherently incomplete, an attacker crafts semantically equivalent but unlisted input (alternate APIs like ctypes or pandas methods, Unicode homoglyphs, parameter-expansion tricks, or unlisted environment variables) to slip past the filter and achieve arbitrary code or command execution in the agent's runtime.
